info.summary: Sunlight absorbed by the Earth system: the engine's fuel.
info.source: ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day: daily sum of hourly accumulations, divided by 86 400 s. Variable: top net solar radiation (tsr, parameter 178).
info.formula: ASR = tsr (incoming minus reflected sunlight at the top of the atmosphere)
info.sign: Positive downward: energy absorbed.
info.meaning: This is the fuel for the heat engine. On global average the Earth absorbs about 240 W m⁻² of sunlight, most of it in the tropics where the sun is high. The difference between tropics and poles is what the atmosphere and oceans work to even out.
info.caveats: Zero in polar night. Clouds change it a lot from day to day.

info.summary: Sunlight absorbed at the surface, heating the ground and the ocean.
info.source: ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day: daily sum of hourly accumulations, divided by 86 400 s. Variable: surface net solar radiation (ssr, parameter 176).
info.formula: R_s = ssr (downward minus reflected sunlight at the surface)
info.sign: Positive downward: energy absorbed.
info.meaning: This heats the engine's hot side. It is the R_s of the maximum-power model: the energy the surface has to get rid of again, by radiation, evaporation and rising warm air.
info.caveats: Depends on modelled clouds and surface reflectivity (snow, ice, desert).

info.summary: Net radiation at the top of the atmosphere: where Earth gains or loses energy.
info.source: ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day: daily sum of hourly accumulations, divided by 86 400 s. Variables: top net solar radiation (tsr, 178) and top net thermal radiation (ttr, 179).
info.formula: N = tsr − OLR, with OLR = −ttr
info.sign: Positive: the Earth system gains energy here. Negative: it loses energy.
info.meaning: The tropics take in more energy than they radiate away and the poles less. The atmosphere and oceans carry the surplus poleward, which is the engine's flow of heat from its hot side to its cold side. The global mean is close to zero.
info.caveats: A single day reflects clouds and weather; the tropical surplus and polar deficit show most clearly in averages.

info.summary: Heat radiated to space: the engine's exhaust.
info.source: ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day: daily sum of hourly accumulations, divided by 86 400 s. Variable: top net thermal radiation (ttr, parameter 179).
info.formula: OLR = −ttr
info.sign: Positive upward: energy leaving the planet. ECMWF stores it as negative; the sign is flipped.
info.meaning: The Earth sheds the sunlight it absorbs as infrared radiation. Warm, dry, cloud-free regions emit most; the cold tops of deep thunderstorm clouds emit least.
info.caveats: Daily mean; it changes with cloud cover from day to day.

info.summary: The temperature at which Earth appears to radiate to space: the engine's cold side.
info.source: Derived from OLR. ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day: daily sum of hourly accumulations, divided by 86 400 s. Variable: ttr (parameter 179).
info.formula: T_e = (OLR / σ)^¼, with σ = 5.670374e-08 W m⁻² K⁻⁴
info.sign: Not applicable (a temperature).
info.meaning: This is the temperature of the engine's cold reservoir. Averaged over the globe it is about 255 K, about 33 K colder than the surface. That gap is the greenhouse effect, and it is the temperature range the atmospheric engine works across.
info.caveats: An effective, blackbody-equivalent temperature, not the temperature of a particular layer. It mixes emission from the surface, water vapour and cloud tops.

info.summary: The Carnot limit: the most work any engine could get from heat flowing to space.
info.source: Derived. ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day. Variables: skin temperature (skt, 235), ttr (179).
info.formula: η_C = (T_s − T_e) / T_s, clamped at 0. T_s is the skin temperature, T_e as in that layer.
info.sign: Not applicable (an efficiency, in %).
info.meaning: Typically 10–20%. It is a theoretical ceiling: the real atmosphere converts far less, because carrying heat away reduces the temperature difference that drives the flow (see the maximum-power layers).
info.caveats: Hatched where the surface is colder than the emission temperature and the limit is clamped at zero, as over cold ice sheets and in polar night. Assumes a reversible engine.

info.summary: The most power convection could generate at this surface (maximum-power model).
info.source: Derived. ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day. Variables: ssr (176), skt (235), ttr (179). Model: Kleidon & Renner (2013).
info.formula: G_max = R_s² / (4 k_r T_s), with k_r = 4 σ T_e³ (T_e clipped to 230–290 K). Reached at J_opt = R_s / 2.
info.sign: Positive: power available to drive motion.
info.meaning: Rising air carries heat away from the surface, which shrinks the temperature difference that drives it. So there is an optimum heat flux, J_opt, at which the power generated peaks. Kleidon argues that convection over land runs close to this maximum.
info.caveats: Single-column model without heat storage, so land only. Absolute values are illustrative and model-based.
info.mask: Ocean and sea ice: the single-column model ignores heat storage, so it is shown over land only.

info.summary: Heat carried up from the surface by rising air and evaporation.
info.source: ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day: daily sum of hourly accumulations, divided by 86 400 s. Variables: surface latent heat flux (slhf, 147), surface sensible heat flux (sshf, 146).
info.formula: J = LE + H, with LE = −slhf and H = −sshf
info.sign: Positive upward: heat leaving the surface. ECMWF stores fluxes as positive downward; the sign is flipped.
info.meaning: This is the engine's actual heat flow out of the surface. Compare it with J_opt, the flux at maximum power (the next layer shows the ratio).
info.caveats: Negative where the surface is colder than the air: at night, in polar regions, over sea ice.

info.summary: Actual surface heat flux ÷ maximum-power flux: is the land near maximum power?
info.source: Derived. ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day. Variables: slhf (147), sshf (146), ssr (176).
info.formula: r_J = (LE + H) / J_opt, with J_opt = R_s / 2
info.sign: A ratio. 1 means the surface runs exactly at maximum power.
info.meaning: Values near 1 mean the land surface sheds heat at about the rate that maximises the power of convection, as the maximum-power view predicts. Values well above or below 1 point to other controls, such as dry soil or heat stored and released.
info.caveats: Model-based. Daily values are affected by heat stored in soil and snow, which the model ignores. Masked where R_s < 10 W m⁻², where J_opt is close to zero.
info.mask: Ocean and sea ice: the single-column model ignores heat storage, so it is shown over land only. Also where there is too little sunlight (R_s < 10 W m⁻²).

info.summary: Latent heat flux: energy carried up in evaporated water.
info.source: ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day: daily sum of hourly accumulations, divided by 86 400 s. Variable: surface latent heat flux (slhf, parameter 147).
info.formula: LE = −slhf
info.sign: Positive upward: heat leaving the surface. ECMWF stores fluxes as positive downward; the sign is flipped.
info.meaning: The main way oceans and wet land shed heat. The energy is released higher up when the vapour condenses, which heats the atmosphere: water vapour is the engine's working fluid.
info.caveats: Negative values mean condensation or frost forming on the surface.

info.summary: Sensible heat flux: heat carried up by warm rising air.
info.source: ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day: daily sum of hourly accumulations, divided by 86 400 s. Variable: surface sensible heat flux (sshf, parameter 146).
info.formula: H = −sshf
info.sign: Positive upward: heat leaving the surface. ECMWF stores fluxes as positive downward; the sign is flipped.
info.meaning: Dominates over deserts and dry land, where there is little water to evaporate.
info.caveats: Negative where the air is warmer than the surface.

info.summary: Share of the surface heat flux that goes into evaporation.
info.source: Derived. ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day: daily sum of hourly accumulations, divided by 86 400 s. Variables: slhf (147), sshf (146).
info.formula: EF = LE / (LE + H)
info.sign: A fraction from 0 (all sensible heat) to 1 (all evaporation).
info.meaning: Close to 1 over oceans and wet vegetation, low over deserts. It shows how much of the engine's heat flow uses water as its working fluid.
info.caveats: Values outside 0–1 occur where H is negative; they are shown at the ends of the scale.
info.mask: Where LE + H is below 10 W m⁻² and the fraction is not meaningful.

info.summary: Wind speed 10 m above the surface.
info.source: ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day: daily mean of hourly values. Variables: 10 m u and v wind (u10, v10; parameters 165, 166).
info.formula: speed = √(u² + v²)
info.sign: Not applicable (a speed).
info.meaning: Part of the engine's mechanical output. Near the surface, friction turns this motion back into heat (see boundary-layer dissipation).
info.caveats: Computed from the day's mean u and v components, so it is the speed of the day's average wind. Where the direction changes during the day it is lower than the average speed.

info.summary: Wind speed 100 m above the surface, about the hub height of wind turbines.
info.source: ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day: daily mean of hourly values. Variables: 100 m u and v wind (u100, v100; parameters 228246, 228247).
info.formula: speed = √(u² + v²)
info.sign: Not applicable (a speed).
info.meaning: The height where wind turbines tap the engine's output, so this is the layer to compare with human energy use.
info.caveats: Computed from the day's mean u and v components, so it is the speed of the day's average wind. Where the direction changes during the day it is lower than the average speed.

info.summary: Jet stream: wind speed at 250 hPa, about 10 km up.
info.source: ERA5 pressure-level daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day: daily mean. Variables: u and v wind at 250 hPa (parameters 131, 132).
info.formula: speed = √(u² + v²)
info.sign: Not applicable (a speed).
info.meaning: The fastest winds, driven by the temperature contrast between tropics and poles. Much of the atmosphere's kinetic energy sits in and around the jets.
info.caveats: Computed from the day's mean u and v components, so it is the speed of the day's average wind. Where the direction changes during the day it is lower than the average speed.

info.summary: Kinetic energy of the air in the whole column.
info.source: ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day: daily mean of hourly values. Variable: vertical integral of kinetic energy (parameter 162059), J m⁻² ÷ 10⁶.
info.formula: KE = ∫ ½ (u² + v²) dp / g, from the surface to the top of the atmosphere
info.sign: Not applicable (always positive).
info.meaning: The engine's store of motion, about 1.5–2 MJ m⁻² on global average. It is topped up by the conversion of heat into motion and drained by friction within days.
info.caveats: Daily mean of hourly values.

info.summary: Boundary-layer dissipation: wind energy turned back into heat by friction.
info.source: ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day: daily sum of hourly accumulations, divided by 86 400 s. Variable: boundary layer dissipation (bld, parameter 145).
info.formula: D_BL = bld
info.sign: Positive: kinetic energy converted to heat.
info.meaning: Over time, the power the engine generates equals the power lost to friction. Summed over the globe this is a few W m⁻²: about 1% of the absorbed sunlight, far below the Carnot limit.
info.caveats: Boundary layer only: friction higher up and gravity-wave drag are not included. It is a model estimate, not a measured quantity.

info.summary: Water vapour in the whole column.
info.source: ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day: daily mean of hourly values. Variable: total column water vapour (tcwv, parameter 137).
info.formula: TCWV = ∫ q dp / g
info.sign: Not applicable (always positive).
info.meaning: Water vapour carries latent heat from where it evaporates to where it condenses. Warm air can hold more: about 7% more per kelvin.
info.caveats: Daily mean of hourly values.

info.summary: Precipitation: where water vapour condensed and released its latent heat.
info.source: ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day: daily sum of hourly accumulations. Variable: total precipitation (tp, parameter 228).
info.formula: P = tp × 1000 (m of water per day → mm per day)
info.sign: Not applicable (always positive).
info.meaning: Each millimetre per day of rain releases about 29 W m⁻² of latent heat into the atmosphere. Rain marks where the engine burns the fuel picked up as evaporation.
info.caveats: Model precipitation, not observed. Below 0.001 mm per day it is shown as the lowest value.

info.summary: Power spent lifting water that falls as rain (indicative).
info.source: Derived from precipitation. ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day. Variable: tp (parameter 228).
info.formula: P_lift = P g h_lift, with g = 9.81 m s⁻² and h_lift = 3000 m
info.sign: Positive: power used to lift water.
info.meaning: Lifting water vapour that later falls as rain uses part of the engine's power, estimated at around 1 W m⁻² globally. That is a large share of the engine's small output.
info.caveats: Indicative only: it assumes all rain is lifted through a fixed 3000 m, a round number. Real lifting heights vary widely.

info.summary: Where the atmosphere exports (positive) or imports (negative) energy.
info.source: ERA5 daily statistics (Copernicus Climate Change Service / ECMWF), UTC day: daily mean of hourly values. Variable: vertical integral of divergence of total energy flux (parameter 162086), smoothed.
info.formula: Smoothed field D_s solves (1 − L² ∇²) D_s = D, with L = 100 km (diffusion on the sphere)
info.sign: Positive: the column exports energy. Negative: it imports energy.
info.meaning: On average the tropics export energy and the poles import it: the transport from the engine's hot side to its cold side.
info.caveats: Daily maps are dominated by weather systems moving energy around; the tropics-to-poles pattern appears in averages. Smoothed to remove grid-scale noise.

info.summary: Energy transported by the atmosphere, from sources to sinks.
info.source: Derived from the smoothed divergence of total energy flux (see that layer). ERA5 parameter 162086.
info.formula: ∇²χ = D_s − ⟨D_s⟩, F = ∇χ (the divergent part of the energy flux)
info.sign: The arrows point the way energy flows. The scalar map shows the size of the flux.
info.meaning: Summed across a latitude circle this matches ERA5's own energy transport: around 5 PW (5 × 10¹⁵ W) poleward in mid-latitudes.
info.caveats: The circulating part of the flux, which moves energy around but carries none across latitude circles, is left out.

info.summary: Human energy use per area.
info.source: Gridded anthropogenic heat flux dataset (to be chosen, see the project's decisions log).
info.formula: q_human, the dataset's annual-mean heat release, regridded to 0.5° by area-weighted averaging
info.sign: Positive: heat released by human energy use.
info.meaning: Humanity uses about 19 TW of primary energy, about 0.04 W m⁻² over the globe, against 240 W m⁻² of absorbed sunlight. Locally, in cities, it is far higher.
info.caveats: Static map, not daily. Dataset and licence still to be confirmed.

info.summary: Human energy use compared with the wind's frictional dissipation.
info.source: Derived: human energy use (see that layer) and ERA5 boundary layer dissipation (bld, 145).
info.formula: r_H = q_human / D_BL
info.sign: A ratio. 1 means human energy use equals the natural dissipation.
info.meaning: Shows where human energy flows rival the power the atmosphere's engine dissipates near the ground.
info.caveats: Human use is static and annual; dissipation is daily.
info.mask: Where boundary-layer dissipation is below 0.01 W m⁻².
